title: Jansenius: what sufficient and efficacious grace mean
source_text: THESIS I. JANSENIUS Episcopus Iprensis, & qui doctrinam illius sequuntur, illam solam gratiam sufficientem vocant, praeter quam nihil aliud ex parte Dei per modum principii necessarium est, ut homo velit & operetur. Gratia vero efficax ea sola illis est, quae naturae creatae non solum dat volendi vires, sed etiam ipsum velle in ea operatur, & volendi facultatem ad volendum ipsa per se flectit & determinat. Adeoque, juxta ipsorum principia, nulla gratia vere sufficiens est, & tamen non efficax, nisi illa quae sic dat creaturae posse velle, ut praeterea nullum divinum auxilium ad volendum praerequiratur; & tamen sic creaturae libertati subdita est, ut penes ejus liberum arbitrium remaneat gratia ista uti vel non uti. Vicissim vero ea sola gratia vere efficax est, non quam quocunque modo sequitur voluntatis actus, sed quae sibi subjicit creaturae voluntatem, eamque ad volendum efficaciter per se movet, ipsum volendi actum vi sua infallibiliter in ea producendo.
pass_a_gloss: THESIS I. Jansenius Bishop of Ypres, and those who follow his doctrine, call that grace alone sufficient, beyond which nothing else on the part of God by way of principle is necessary, that man may will and work. But efficacious grace is to them that alone, which not only gives to created nature the strength of willing, but also works in it the willing itself, and bends and determines by itself the faculty of willing to will. And so, according to their own principles, no grace is truly sufficient, and yet not efficacious, except that which so gives to the creature the being able to will, that besides no divine help to will is prerequired; and yet is so subject to the liberty of the creature, that it remains in the power of its free choice to use or not use that grace. And conversely that grace alone is truly efficacious, not which the act of the will follows in whatever way, but which subjects to itself the will of the creature, and moves it efficaciously by itself to will, by its own force infallibly producing in it the very act of willing.
pass_b_english: Thesis I. Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, and his followers give the name sufficient grace only to a grace after which God need supply nothing further, by way of principle, for a person to will and act. Efficacious grace, for them, is only the grace that does more than give created nature the strength to will: it produces the willing itself in that nature, and of itself bends and determines the faculty of will to will.

On their principles, then, no grace is truly sufficient and yet not efficacious except one that gives the creature the ability to will so fully that no further divine help toward willing is needed beforehand, and that is yet so subject to the creature's freedom that whether to use that grace or not rests with its free choice. Conversely, the only truly efficacious grace is not one that the will's act happens to follow somehow, but one that brings the creature's will under itself, moves it of itself effectively to will, and by its own force infallibly produces the act of willing in it.
